title: The Khmer Empire and Angkor's Water City

cards.h: A city the size of a country
cards.b:
Angkor, in today's Cambodia, was one of the largest pre-industrial cities on Earth. Its temples, canals and reservoirs were built by the Khmer Empire between the 800s and the 1400s.

Most of Angkor's people lived in wooden houses that have long since rotted away. What survives is stone, and stone can mislead us about how big the city really was.

cards.h: A king who claimed the gods
cards.b:
Around 802 CE a young prince named Jayavarman II proclaimed himself a universal king on a mountain called Mahendraparvata, now Phnom Kulen. He created a royal cult, the devaraja, which tied the king to the god Shiva.

The Khmer kings then built an empire that stretched across much of mainland Southeast Asia. Their power rested on rice, labour and water, and on Sanskrit culture that came by sea from India.

cards.h: Angkor Wat, the temple of Vishnu
cards.b:
Suryavarman II (reigned about 1113 to 1150) built Angkor Wat, dedicated to the god Vishnu. It is one of the largest religious monuments in the world, surrounded by a moat about five kilometres around.

Its walls carry long carved reliefs, including a procession of the king and scenes from Hindu epics. The temple was built as a model of the universe, with the central peak representing Mount Meru.

Zhou Daguan (visit 1296–1297)

A Chinese envoy sent to the Khmer court, Zhou wrote Customs of Cambodia. He describes markets, houses, clothes and the way people traded with Chinese merchants.

He is our best eyewitness of Angkor at its height. His notes are short, but they show a busy city full of trade and daily life.

cards.h: The Khmer story in five dates
cards.b: The dates show a line from a new kingdom to a great temple state, and then to its slow decline and its loss to the Thai kingdom of Ayutthaya.

Jayavarman VII ruled around 1181 to about 1218. He built the great temple of the Bayon at the centre of Angkor Thom, with its towers of smiling faces, and he rebuilt much of the empire after wars with the Cham kingdom.

Inscriptions say he founded many rest houses and hospitals, around a hundred of them, along the royal roads. Historians see this as a sign of a king who wanted to be seen as caring for the sick and travellers.

Angkor's kings dug huge reservoirs called barays. The East Baray was several kilometres long. They stored monsoon water for rice fields and for the dry season, and canals linked the city to the wider landscape.

Water was power in Angkor. A king who could feed his people through the dry season could hold his followers together. Historians now treat the water system as one of the most impressive engineering feats of its age.

A popular image shows Angkor overgrown by jungle, abandoned by a people who simply walked away. It made a great story when French explorers found the ruins in the 1860s.

Historians argue the real story is more complex. Droughts, floods, shifting rivers, war with Ayutthaya and changing religion all played a part. The water system may have failed under extreme monsoon swings, but the causes are still debated.

In 1431 the armies of Ayutthaya, the Thai kingdom to the west, sacked Angkor. Much of the court moved south, and in the following decades the capital shifted towards what is now Phnom Penh.

Angkor did not disappear. Monks kept the temples in use, and later kings were crowned there. But the royal city was no longer the centre of power.

Angkor Wat appears on the Cambodian flag, and the temple complex is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its stone carvings show the wide reach of Indian ideas in Southeast Asia.

Modern Cambodians see Angkor as a source of national pride. Historians argue about how to present the story, since it was built by thousands of workers, many of them forced to labour for the state.

In about 1025 the Chola king Rajendra I sent a naval expedition across the Bay of Bengal. It attacked the ports of Srivijaya in Sumatra, the sea power that controlled much of the trade with the Khmer lands.

The Khmer court took Sanskrit as its learned language, and its kings carved the Ramayana and Mahabharata into stone. Indian stories were part of the everyday culture of Angkor.

Five things to remember
  1. The Khmer Empire grew from the early 800s.
  2. Angkor Wat was built for Vishnu under Suryavarman II.
  3. Zhou Daguan left the best eyewitness account of the city.
  4. Reservoirs (barays) were the engine of rice production.
  5. Ayutthaya sacked Angkor in 1431.
Think about it
  • How much of Angkor's fall came from nature, and how much from people?
  • Why did a temple state need so many workers?
